claim: Nitrogen is part of 75% of the cell's building blocks, mainly in proteins and nucleic acids.
source: Nitrogen is essential for all forms of life as it is part of 75% of the cell's building blocks (mainly in proteins and nucleic acids) (Milo and Phillips, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milo and Phillips, 2015.

claim: Ammonium enters metabolism solely via glutamate dehydrogenase and the combined activity of glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase.
source: As ammonium enters metabolism solely via these two routes, all cellular nitrogen is provided by either glutamate (75%) or glutamine (25%) (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: All cellular nitrogen is provided by either glutamate (75%) or glutamine (25%).
source: As ammonium enters metabolism solely via these two routes, all cellular nitrogen is provided by either glutamate (75%) or glutamine (25%) (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: The glutamate auxotrophic strain (glut-aux, ΔgdhA ΔgltBD) was not able to grow in minimal medium with ammonium as the sole nitrogen source unless an amine group donor, such as glutamate, was provided in the medium.
source: The resulting glutamate auxotrophic strain (glut-aux, ΔgdhA ΔgltBD) was not able to grow in minimal medium with ammonium as the sole nitrogen source unless an amine group donor, such as glutamate, was provided in the medium (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Aspartate, leucine, and tyrosine serving as cellular amine donor for glutamate generation from 2-ketoglutarate could be attributed to the activity of aspartate transaminase (AspC), tyrosine transaminase (TryB), and branched-chain amino acid transaminase (IlvE).
source: For example, aspartate, leucine, and tyrosine serving as cellular amine donor for glutamate generation from 2-ketoglutarate (rescue mechanism II, Figure 1) could be attributed to the activity of aspartate transaminase (AspC), tyrosine transaminase (TryB), and branched-chain amino acid transaminase (IlvE) (Gelfand and Steinberg, 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gelfand and Steinberg, 1977.

claim: The [glutamate]/[2-ketoglutarate] ratio is very high (above 100) under physiological conditions.
source: While transaminases are generally reversible enzymes, their ability to effectively operate reversibly in vivo is not trivial as the [glutamate]/[2-ketoglutarate] ratio is very high (above 100) under physiological conditions (Bennett et al., 2009), making the reverse amine transfer onto 2-ketoglutarate to form glutamate thermodynamically challenging.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bennett et al., 2009.

claim: Most of the amino acids were completely unlabeled when the glut-aux strain was cultivated with unlabeled amino acids in medium containing 15N-ammonium, confirming that their amine group was transferred from the respective amine-donating amino acid rather than from free ammonia in the medium.
source: In these experiments, we found that most of the amino acids were completely unlabeled (Figure 3A), confirming that their amine group was transferred from the respective amine-donating amino acid rather than from free (15N labeled) ammonia in the medium (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Arginine appeared single-labeled as one of its nitrogen atoms originates from the amide nitrogen of glutamine that is derived from ammonia fixed by GS activity.
source: In these experiments, arginine appeared single-labeled (R, Figure 3) as one of its nitrogen atoms originates from the amide nitrogen of glutamine that is derived from ammonia fixed by GS activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and the schematic in Figure 3B.

claim: Biomass yield, as indicated by the maximal OD600, directly correlated with the concentration of the supplemented amino acid.
source: As expected, we found that biomass yield, as indicated by the maximal OD600, directly correlated with the concentration of the supplemented amino acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ornithine supported roughly double the yield for each concentration compared to other amino acids.
source: All amino acids showed the same dependency of biomass yield on concentration, with the exception of ornithine, which supported roughly double the yield for each concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transaminases can transfer both amine groups from the ornithine degradation intermediate putrescine to 2-ketoglutarate to form glutamate.
source: This is in line with the fact that transaminases can transfer both amine groups from the ornithine degradation intermediate putrescine to 2-ketoglutarate to form glutamate (Prieto-Santos et al., 1986) (rescue mechanism III, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prieto-Santos et al., 1986.

claim: Glutamate was not the amine donor supporting fastest growth of the glut-aux strain.
source: To our surprise, glutamate was not the amine donor supporting fastest growth of the glut-aux strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Proline supported faster growth than glutamate despite needing to be converted to glutamate to donate its amine group.
source: Even proline, which, in order to donate its amine group, needs to be converted to glutamate (rescue mechanism IV, Figure 1), supported faster growth (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Glutamate uptake is limiting growth of the glut-aux strain.
source: This, together with the fact that the growth rate increased proportionally with the glutamate concentration, indicates that glutamate uptake is limiting growth of the glut-aux strain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations of growth rate dependence on glutamate concentration.

claim: Proline is metabolized by PutA to glutamate.
source: We did not expect this amino acid to donate its amine group directly, but rather to be metabolized by PutA, encoding for a bifunctional flavoenzyme with proline dehydrogenase and 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase activities (Moxley et al., 2014), to glutamate (Frank and Ranhand, 1964), which would serve as an amine source (rescue mechanism IV, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moxley et al., 2014 and Frank and Ranhand, 1964.

claim: Deletion of putA abolished growth of the WT and glut-aux strain on proline as the sole ammonium source.
source: Indeed, upon deletion of putA, growth of the WT and glut-aux strain on proline as the sole ammonium source was abolished (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of ybdL in the ΔgdhA ΔgltBD strain did not affect growth with methionine as an amine donor.
source: However, deletion of ybdL in the ΔgdhA ΔgltBD strain did not affect growth with methionine as an amine donor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the physiological contribution of this transaminase to the use of methionine as an amine source is negligible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glut-aux ΔybdL strain did not show any growth retardation when using histidine or phenylalanine as an amine donor.
source: Yet, the glut-aux ΔybdL strain did not show any growth retardation when using histidine or phenylalanine as an amine donor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glut-aux ΔaspC strain was unable to grow with histidine, tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine as amine donors.
source: We found that the glut-aux ΔaspC strain was unable to grow with histidine, tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine as amine donors, which all allowed growth of the glut-aux strain (gray lines in Figure 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 5B.

claim: AspC is essential for the utilization of histidine, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine as amine donors in vivo.
source: Although AspC had shown low specific transaminase activity with histidine, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine in vitro (Hayashi et al., 1993), our experiments suggest, however, that the enzyme is essential for the utilization of these amino acids as amine donors in vivo (rescue mechanisms II or III, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to Hayashi et al., 1993.

claim: Alanine did not serve as an amine source for the glut-aux strain, regardless of the presence or absence of ammonia in the medium.
source: Despite the presence of two glutamate-producing alanine transaminases (AlaA, AlaC) as well as multiple transaminases that can promiscuously accept alanine (Kim et al., 2010; Peña-Soler et al., 2014), alanine did not serve as an amine source for the glut-aux strain, regardless of the presence or absence of ammonia in the medium (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Peña-Soler et al., 2014.

claim: Overexpression of the alanine transaminase isozymes AlaA and AlaC did not enable growth with alanine as an amine donor.
source: Even upon overexpression of the alanine transaminase isozymes AlaA and AlaC, no growth with alanine as an amine donor was observed (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Two cultures of the glut-aux strain overexpressing AlaA could use alanine as an amine donor after prolonged incubation, arising after 110 and 133 hr.
source: Indeed, in this experiment two cultures of the glut-aux strain overexpressing AlaA could use alanine as an amine donor. These spontaneous mutants arose after a cultivation time of 110 and 133 hr, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both isolates that could grow on alanine had mutations in the alanine racemase gene dadX.
source: Analysis of the genome sequencing results revealed that both isolates had mutations in the alanine racemase gene dadX (Supplementary file 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deletion of dadX in the glut-aux strain overexpressing AlaA allowed immediate growth with alanine as an amine donor.
source: To verify this hypothesis, we deleted dadX in the evolved strain, as well as in the parental glut-aux strain. Both strains (with overexpression of AlaA) immediately grew with alanine as an amine donor (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), verifying that reducing an important intracellular alanine sink allowed the overexpressed transaminase to use alanine as an amine donor to effectively sustain growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of DadA in the glut-aux strain overexpressing AlaA did not restore growth with alanine as an amine donor.
source: Noteworthy, a deletion of DadA in the glut-aux strain overexpressing AlaA did not restore growth with alanine as an amine donor, indicating that the reversible conversion of l-alanine to d-alanine is already sufficient to reduce alanine availability below a critical level, where it cannot support enough flux via AlaA for cellular growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: β-alanine is neither a suitable amine donor for the glut-aux strain nor an N-source for the wildtype.
source: The non-proteinogenic amino acid β-alanine is neither a suitable amine donor for the glut-aux strain nor an N-source for the wildtype (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of either BaPAT or BaOAT allowed the wildtype strain to grow using β-alanine as the sole source of ammonia.
source: Overexpression of either BaPAT or BaOAT allowed the wildtype strain to grow using β-alanine as the sole source of ammonia (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The glut-aux strain was only able to grow with β-alanine as an amine donor when BaOAT, but not BaPAT, was overexpressed.
source: The glut-aux strain however was only able to grow with β-alanine as an amine donor when BaOAT, but not BaPAT, was overexpressed (Figure 6B), which is in good agreement with our previous results that glutamate, but not alanine, can immediately serve as an amine donor in the glut-aux strain (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 2.

claim: The majority of amino acids did not show any 15N labeling when the glut-aux + BaOAT strain was grown on 15N-labeled ammonium with β-alanine, confirming that their amino group originated from β-alanine.
source: As expected, the majority of amino acids did not show any 15N labeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), confirming that their amino group originated from β-alanine, rather than from ammonium.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Glycine did not serve as an amine source in the glut-aux strain.
source: Like alanine, glycine did not serve as an amine source in the glut-aux strain (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Growth of the glut-aux strain overexpressing BhcA was not restored upon supplying the medium with glycine.
source: However, growth of the glut-aux strain overexpressing BhcA was not restored upon supplying the medium with glycine (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Deletion of dadA allowed the glut-aux strain overexpressing BhcA to grow slowly with glycine as an amine donor.
source: Indeed, the deletion of dadA allowed the strain to grow slowly with glycine as an amine donor (Figure 6C), at first indicating glycine removal via promiscuous activity of DadA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DadA showed only a very low specific activity with glycine in vitro.
source: However, in vitro, DadA showed only a very low specific activity with glycine (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A) and an apparent KM > 500 mM for this amino acid (Supplementary file 3), which strongly suggested that the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM of 0.275 M–1 s–1) of the enzyme (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A, Supplementary file 3) was insufficient to provide a strong glycine sink in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: In vitro measurements of DadA confirmed a higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM of 5.71 M–1 s–1) with d-serine than with glycine.
source: In vitro measurements of DadA confirmed a higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM of 5.71 M–1 s–1) of DadA with d-serine (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A) than previously measured with glycine.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A.

claim: BhcA exhibits much better kinetic properties with serine (KM 2.1 mM; kcat 8.8 s–1) than with glycine.
source: BhcA exhibits much better kinetic properties with serine (tested with glyoxylate as the acceptor [KM 2.1 mM; kcat 8.8 s–1]) than with glycine (Schada von Borzyskowski et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schada von Borzyskowski et al., 2019.

claim: Deletion of the GCV subunits gcvTHP in the glut-aux strain overexpressing BhcA did not allow growth with glycine.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the deletion of the GCV subunits gcvTHP in the glut-aux strain overexpressing BhcA did not allow growth with glycine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Deletion of gcvTHP in the glut-aux ∆dadA strain overexpressing BhcA abolished growth with glycine.
source: Moreover, deletion of gcvTHP in the glut-aux ∆dadA strain overexpressing BhcA abolished growth with glycine (Figure 6C), providing strong evidence that glycine is converted to serine to utilize it as an amine donor (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: Growth of the glut-aux, glut-aux ∆dadA, glut-aux ∆gcvTHP, and glut-aux ∆dadA ∆gcvTHP strains (all overexpressing BhcA) was restored upon addition of low serine concentrations.
source: In good agreement with the conclusion of our glycine trials, we found that the growth of the glut-aux, glut-aux ∆dadA, glut-aux ∆gcvTHP, and glut-aux ∆dadA ∆gcvTHP strains (all overexpressing BhcA) was restored upon addition of low serine concentrations (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Serine concentrations above 1.7 mM seemed to be toxic to the strain.
source: In our growth experiments, serine concentrations above 1.7 mM seemed to be toxic to the strain, which can be explained by the inhibition of isoleucine and aromatic amino acid biosynthesis by serine-derived hydroxypyruvate (Hama et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Hama et al., 1990.

claim: The glut-aux ∆dadA reached the highest OD600 on all tested serine concentrations.
source: The glut-aux ∆dadA reached the highest OD600 on all tested serine concentrations, indicating that also here deletion of DadA is beneficial as it removes a sink for either glycine or serine directly (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In vitro measurements with purified BhcA confirmed amine transfer from serine to oxaloacetate with a KM of 7 mM and a kcat of 25.9 s–1.
source: The enzymatic coupling assay indeed confirmed amine transfer from serine to oxaloacetate (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B, Supplementary file 3). The resulting KM of 7 mM and a kcat of 25.9 s–1 (Supplementary file 3) indicated a sufficient turnover of serine and oxaloacetate into aspartate and hydroxypyruvate.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Aspartate, proline, serine, alanine, and glycine were unlabeled in the glut-aux ΔdadA strain overexpressing BhcA grown on 15NH4 with glycine or serine, confirming that all amines were derived only from the provided amino acid.
source: Aspartate, proline, serine, alanine, and glycine were unlabeled in the glut-aux ΔdadA strain overexpressing BhcA, confirming that indeed all amines were derived only from the provided amino acid and not from free ammonium in the medium (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: Aspartate allowed fastest growth of all amino acids tested for the glut-aux strain.
source: Both aspartate and leucine previously were amine sources for the glut-aux strain, but while aspartate allowed fastest growth of all amino acids tested, leucine supported only very slow growth (Figure 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The thermodynamics of the aspartate ammonia lyase reaction reveal a full reversibility with a ΔrG'm of 4 [kJ/mol] in the aspartate-forming direction.
source: However, the thermodynamics of this reaction reveal a full reversibility with a ΔrG'm of 4 [kJ/mol] (in the aspartate-forming direction at a concentration of 1 mM for all reactants; http://equilibrator.weizmann.ac.il/).
evidence: The claim is supported by thermodynamic calculations from equilibrator.weizmann.ac.il.

claim: Growth of the glut-aux strain overexpressing AspA (+AspA) was observed on all tested carbon sources.
source: Growth of the glut-aux strain overexpressing AspA (+AspA) was indeed observed on all tested carbon sources (Figure 7A), suggesting that aspartate and AspA can replace the canonical glutamate-based ammonium assimilation pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The glut-aux + AspA strain grew fastest on carbon sources closest to fumarate (2-ketoglutarate, succinate, malate, fumarate).
source: The glut-aux + AspA strain grew fastest on carbon sources closest to fumarate, the substrate of AspA (2-ketoglutarate, succinate, malate, fumarate).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The WT and the glut-aux + AspA strain showed identical 15N labeling when grown on 20 mM succinate with 15NH4 or 14NH4.
source: Here, the WT and the glut-aux + AspA strain, showed identical labeling (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Growth of the glut-aux strain was observed only upon supplementation with catalytic amounts of MOP when LeuDH was overexpressed.
source: Consequently, we observed growth of the glut-aux strain only upon supplementation with catalytic amounts of MOP, which served as ammonium acceptor in the amination reaction catalyzed by LeuDH (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The glut-aux strain overexpressing B. cereus LeuDH growing on glycerol and 0.2 and 0.5 mM MOP reached twice the OD600 obtained for the glut-aux strain growing on glycerol and 5 mM leucine.
source: The glut-aux strain overexpressing B. cereus LeuDH growing on glycerol and 0.2 and 0.5 mM MOP reached twice the OD600 obtained for the glut-aux strain growing on glycerol and 5 mM leucine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The observed single label for the analyzed amino acids alanine, phenylalanine, methionine, proline, serine, and threonine confirms operation of the LeuDH's ammonium entry point.
source: The observed single label for the analyzed amino acids alanine, phenylalanine, methionine, proline, serine, and threonine once again confirms operation of the LeuDH's ammonium entry point (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The glut-aux strain did not grow on all tested amino acids.
source: Our experiments revealed that the glut-aux did not grow on all tested amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The substrate spectrum of the underlying amination network might be larger than identified by the experiments since for some amino acids uptake might limit their intracellular availability.
source: Here, we note that the substrate spectrum of the underlying amination network might be larger than identified by our experiments since for some amino acids we cannot rule out that their uptake limits their intracellular availability to the network.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental limitations.

claim: Use of threonine as nitrogen source would require induction of threonine dehydrogenase by the presence of leucine.
source: For example, use of threonine as nitrogen source would require induction of threonine dehydrogenase by the presence of leucine (Potter et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Potter et al., 1977.

claim: Growth in the presence of valine was shown to be inhibited due to valine-dependent inhibition of acetohydroxy acid synthase essential to isoleucine biosynthesis.
source: Growth in the presence of valine was shown to be inhibited due to valine-dependent inhibition of acetohydroxy acid synthase essential to isoleucine biosynthesis (Tuite et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tuite et al., 2005.

claim: Absence of nitrogen from the medium only affected growth of the glut-aux on ornithine.
source: As absence of nitrogen from the medium only affected growth of the glut-aux on ornithine, we concluded that nitrogen response-dependent regulation was of minor relevance for amino acid metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Intracellular glutamate levels are expected to be lower in the glut-aux strain than in a wildtype strain under saturating nitrogen availability.
source: Given the inability of the selection strain to synthesize glutamate, intracellular glutamate levels are expected to be lower than in a wildtype strain under saturating nitrogen availability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic modifications in the glut-aux strain.

claim: Deletion of AspC alone was sufficient to abolish growth of the glut-aux strain on tyrosine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, and leucine.
source: First, deletion of AspC alone was sufficient to abolish growth of the glut-aux strain on tyrosine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, and leucine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of AspC abolished growth on histidine, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine for which only low or no specific activity of AspC was reported in vitro.
source: Second, deletion of AspC abolished growth on histidine, methionine, isoleucine, and leucine for which only low or no specific activity of AspC was reported in vitro (Hayashi et al., 1993; Powell and Morrison, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study and citations to Hayashi et al., 1993 and Powell and Morrison, 1978.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the substrate range of AspC seems to be broader than previously anticipated.
source: Under physiological conditions, the substrate range of AspC thus seems to be broader than previously anticipated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations in this study.

claim: The glut-aux ΔaspC strain was unable to grow with tryptophan as an amine source.
source: Third, the glut-aux ΔaspC strain was unable to grow with tryptophan as an amine source.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the glut-aux strain, tryptophan is the direct substrate of AspC to form (indole-3-yl)-pyruvate and glutamate.
source: We hence conclude that in the glut-aux strain, tryptophan is the direct substrate of AspC to form (indole-3-yl)-pyruvate and glutamate as in some bacteria (e.g., P. aeruginosa [Bortolotti et al., 2016], Clostridium sporogenes [O'Neil and DeMoss, 1968]), protozoa (Trichomonas vaginalis [Lowe and Rowe, 1985]), or mammals (Shrawder and Martinez-Carrion, 1972).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations and supported by citations to Bortolotti et al., 2016, O'Neil and DeMoss, 1968, Lowe and Rowe, 1985, and Shrawder and Martinez-Carrion, 1972.

claim: The majority of amino acids suggested to be used via direct transamination rescued the glut-aux strain, but were not a good amine source for the wildtype.
source: Grouping amino acids by expected rescue mechanism and rescue phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) revealed that the majority of amino acids we suggest to be used via direct transamination rescued the glut-aux strain, but were not a good amine source for the wildtype (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AspC is essential for the growth of the glut-aux on all amino acids not supporting WT growth.
source: Additionally, we found AspC to be essential for the growth of the glut-aux on all amino acids not supporting WT growth (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Promiscuous transaminase activity is one mechanism for adaptation to lacking glutamate availability.
source: Therefore, we suggest promiscuous transaminase activity here rescuing growth of the glut-aux. strain to be one mechanism for adaptation to lacking glutamate availability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations in this study.

claim: Overexpression of alanine-2-ketoglutarate aminotransferase, together with the removal of an alanine sink, allowed usage of alanine as an amine source.
source: Overexpression of alanine-2-ketoglutarate aminotransferase, together with the removal of an alanine sink, allowed usage of alanine as an amine source.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: By overexpressing transaminases that transfer amines from β-alanine to 2-ketoglutarate, usage of the non-proteinogenic amino acid β-alanine as amine source was engineered.
source: By overexpressing transaminases that transfer amines from β-alanine to 2-ketoglutarate, we engineered usage of the non-proteinogenic amino acid β-alanine as amine source.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Upon deletion of the d-amino acid dehydrogenase gene dadA, the engineered strain was able to use the amine from glycine to support growth.
source: Upon deletion of the d-amino acid dehydrogenase gene dadA as potential internal sink for glycine and serine, the engineered strain was able to use the amine from glycine to support growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The strain did not use glycine directly, but converted it to serine.
source: Surprisingly, we discovered that the strain did not use glycine directly, but converted it to serine, which was yet another substrate of the transaminase showing high activity for serine (kcat of 25.87 s–1) with oxaloacetate as amine acceptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The newly discovered serine-oxaloacetate transaminase activity can be coupled to formate assimilation via the reductive glycine pathway.
source: In principle, the newly discovered serine-oxaloacetate transaminase activity can be coupled to formate assimilation via the reductive glycine pathway (Kim et al., 2020), which fixes ammonium by reverse activity of the glycine cleavage system.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental findings and a citation to Kim et al., 2020.

claim: For alanine, β-alanine, glycine, and serine, transaminase availability was the main bottleneck rather than transport or regulatory issues.
source: Thus, we conclude that for these amino acids, transaminase availability was the main bottleneck rather than transport or regulatory issues.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations in this study.

claim: The glut-aux strain is an excellent selection platform to screen for any reaction that produces amino acids which can rescue growth.
source: In addition to this finding, these examples demonstrate the glut-aux strain as an excellent selection platform to screen for any reaction that produces amino acids which can rescue growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental design and results of this study.

claim: Both fumarate amination to aspartate and MOP amination to leucine reconstituted the ability of the glut-aux strain to assimilate free ammonium.
source: Both fumarate amination to aspartate and MOP amination to leucine reconstituted the ability of the glut-aux strain to assimilate free ammonium.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Growth dependent on ammonium assimilation via AspA was fastest when a carbon source metabolically close to fumarate was provided.
source: Growth dependent on ammonium assimilation via AspA was fastest when a carbon source metabolically close to fumarate was provided.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ammonium assimilation via aspartate ammonia lyase requires NADH for the reduction of oxaloacetate back to fumarate, while glutamate-dependent amination requires NADPH consumption by glutamate dehydrogenase.
source: We note that assimilation of ammonium via aspartate ammonia lyase is energetically different from ammonium assimilation via glutamate. While a glutamate-dependent amination network requires NADPH consumption by glutamate dehydrogenase, an aspartate ammonia lyase-dependent network requires NADH for the reduction of oxaloacetate back to fumarate; oxaloacetate being the transamination product of aspC.
evidence: The claim is based on metabolic reasoning and knowledge of the pathways.

claim: NADH is energetically cheaper compared to NADPH as the recovery of the latter from NADH wastes some proton motive force through the membrane-bound transhydrogenase.
source: NADH is energetically cheaper compared to NADPH as the recovery of the latter from NADH wastes some proton motive force through the membrane-bound transhydrogenase, and hence comes with the indirect cost of ATP synthesis (Spaans et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spaans et al., 2015.

claim: GDH and GS are kinetically superior to AspA or LeuDH under ammonium-limiting conditions, with KM values of 2 mM and 0.1 mM for ammonia, respectively, compared to 20 mM and 13 mM for AspA and LeuDH.
source: Under ammonium-limiting conditions, GDH and GS are kinetically superior with a KM of 2 mM and 0.1 mM for ammonia, respectively (Reitzer, 2014), compared to AspA or LeuDH from B. cereus with KM values of 20 mM and 13 mM for ammonia, respectively (Suzuki et al., 1973; Sanwal and Zink, 1961).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reitzer, 2014, Suzuki et al., 1973, and Sanwal and Zink, 1961.

claim: The availability of two different systems (GDH and GS/GOGAT), which are each optimal for different growth conditions but generate the same molecule, is unique to glutamate-based ammonium assimilation.
source: Additionally, the availability of two different systems (GDH and GS/GOGAT), which are each optimal for different growth conditions but generate the same molecule, is unique to glutamate-based ammonium assimilation.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of metabolic pathways.

claim: Growth of the engineered strains under nonoptimal conditions would likely be impaired by a lack of flexible metabolic responses to varying nitrogen and energy availability.
source: It is even likely that growth of the engineered strains under nonoptimal conditions would be impaired by a lack of flexible metabolic responses to varying nitrogen and energy availability.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on metabolic principles.

claim: Regulatory effects, for example, GS inhibition by several amino acids (e.g., tryptophan, histidine, alanine, glycine), might explain why some amino acids only supported slow growth of the glut-aux strain.
source: Furthermore, regulatory effects, for example, GS inhibition by several amino acids (e.g., tryptophan, histidine, alanine, glycine), might explain why some amino acids only supported slow growth of the glut-aux strain (Hubbard and Stadtman, 1967).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by a citation to Hubbard and Stadtman, 1967.

claim: The underlying metabolic network for amination is highly flexible.
source: The possibility to modify ammonium assimilation and metabolism by metabolic engineering indicates that the underlying metabolic network is highly flexible, which is supported by highly promiscuous transaminases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results of this study.

claim: Transaminases are a limiting factor that defines the amination network.
source: However, transaminases are a limiting factor that defines the amination network, which implies the presence of different amination networks in different organisms that express different transaminases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results of this study.

claim: Amino acid usage and even ammonium assimilation mechanisms are transferable by expressing heterologous genes.
source: That said, our study demonstrates how amino acid usage and even ammonium assimilation mechanisms are transferable by expressing heterologous genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in this study.

claim: The amine distribution network around the universally conserved core principle of glutamate-based amine assimilation must be highly flexible to allow transferability between apparently different amination networks.
source: In this, we find that to allow such transferability between apparently different amination networks, the amine distribution network around the universally conserved core principle of glutamate-based amine assimilation must be highly flexible.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results of this study.

claim: Engineering ammonium assimilation via non-glutamate-producing reactions can decouple cellular ammonium assimilation from glutamate biosynthesis for the production of nitrogenous compounds.
source: By engineering ammonium assimilation via non-glutamate-producing reactions, the cellular ammonium assimilation can be decoupled from glutamate biosynthesis for the production of nitrogenous compounds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results of this study.

claim: Metabolic network optimization was previously demonstrated by increased arginine production yields in Corynebacterium glutamicum upon expression of E. coli AspA and GlnA.
source: For example, such metabolic network optimization was previously demonstrated by increased arginine production yields in Corynebacterium glutamicum upon expression of E. coli AspA and GlnA (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: E. coli acquires higher growth rates with glycerol as carbon and energy source when amino acids are provided as amine sources.
source: Moreover, previous studies showed that E. coli acquires higher growth rates with glycerol as carbon and energy source when amino acids are provided as amine sources (Bren et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bren et al., 2016.

claim: Aspartate immediately supported fastest growth of the glut-aux strain.
source: To minimize selective pressure in the preculture and avoid accumulation of mutations prior to the experiment, all experiments were inoculated from cultures grown in glycerol minimal medium supplemented with 5 mM aspartate, the amino acid immediately supporting fastest growth of the glut-aux strain (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In E. coli, ornithine is degraded to putrescine, which is used by the transaminase PatA to aminate 2-ketoglutarate to glutamate.
source: In E. coli, ornithine is degraded to putrescine, which is used by the transaminase PatA to aminate 2-ketoglutarate to glutamate (Schneider et al., 2013; Schneider and Reitzer, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schneider et al., 2013 and Schneider and Reitzer, 2012.

claim: Expression of the ornithine degradation pathway is induced by nitrogen limitation.
source: Expression of this degradation pathway is induced by nitrogen limitation (Zimmer et al., 2000) and allows growth with ornithine (rescue mechanism III, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zimmer et al., 2000.

claim: The glut-aux strain represents the first strain for a systematic investigation of the metabolic network for amine distribution.
source: While d-glutamate-requiring E. coli mutants had been previously characterized (Dougherty et al., 1993), our strain lacking glutamate biosynthetic pathways represents the first strain for a systematic investigation of the metabolic network for amine distribution.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dougherty et al., 1993 and the novelty of the current study.

claim: Three cooperating canonical enzymes assimilate ammonium in two distinct ways at the node between 2-ketoglutarate, glutamate, and glutamine.
source: Here, three cooperating canonical enzymes assimilate ammonium in two distinct ways.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ammonium assimilation pathways.

claim: Glutamate is the direct product of glutamate dehydrogenase (gdhA, GDH).
source: In the first reaction, glutamate is the direct product of glutamate dehydrogenase (gdhA, GDH).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the GDH reaction.

claim: The combined activity of glutamine synthetase (glnA, GS) and glutamate synthase (glutamine 2-ketoglutarate aminotransferase, gltBD, GOGAT) fixes ammonium and converts glutamate into glutamine, which then donates one amine to 2-ketoglutarate to form two glutamate molecules.
source: In the second pathway, the combined activity of glutamine synthetase (glnA, GS) and glutamate synthase (glutamine 2-ketoglutarate aminotransferase, gltBD, GOGAT) fixes another ammonium and converts glutamate into glutamine, which then donates one amine to 2-ketoglutarate to form two glutamate molecules (Helling, 1994; Kumar and Shimizu, 2010; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Helling, 1994 and Kumar and Shimizu, 2010, and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most of the GS orthologs have evolved kinetic parameters optimized for lower ammonium concentrations with an apparent KM of 0.1 mM for ammonium.
source: Additionally, most of the GS orthologs have evolved kinetic parameters optimized for lower ammonium concentrations with an apparent KM of 0.1 mM for ammonium (Reitzer, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reitzer, 2014.

claim: At high ammonium concentrations, the NADPH-dependent GDH allows more efficient ammonium assimilation than GS.
source: At high ammonium concentrations, the NADPH-dependent (and thus energetically cheaper) GDH allows more efficient ammonium assimilation than GS (Reitzer, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reitzer, 2014.

claim: To generate the NADPH required for GDH, Escherichia coli mostly uses the membrane-bound proton-translocating transhydrogenase (PntAB).
source: To generate the NADPH required for GDH, Escherichia coli mostly uses the membrane-bound proton-translocating transhydrogenase (PntAB) (Sauer et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sauer et al., 2004.

claim: The membrane-bound proton-translocating transhydrogenase exploits the proton motif force to drive proton translocation from NADH to NADP+.
source: This enzyme exploits the proton motif force to drive proton translocation from NADH to NADP+ (Spaans et al., 2015), and thereby indirectly competes with ATP synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spaans et al., 2015.

claim: When growing under high ammonium concentrations, growth of E. coli might benefit from ammonium assimilation via NADH-dependent dehydrogenases.
source: Therefore, when growing under high ammonium concentrations, growth of this microorganism might benefit from ammonium assimilation via NADH-dependent dehydrogenases.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on metabolic principles.

claim: Alternative entry points for ammonium theoretically exist, for example, alanine dehydrogenase or aspartate ammonia lyase, but these are not relevant for ammonium assimilation.
source: Besides the glutamate biosynthesis node, alternative entry points for ammonium theoretically exist, for example, alanine dehydrogenase or aspartate ammonia lyase, but these are not relevant for ammonium assimilation (Kim and Hollocher, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim and Hollocher, 1982.

claim: The ATP investment driving GS activity makes amination reactions favorable even at low ammonium concentrations.
source: The ATP investment driving GS activity makes amination reactions favorable even at low ammonium concentrations.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of enzyme kinetics and thermodynamics.
